check: independently verify goal item 4, the fault matrix, rather than citing the ledger row that says PASS
why: The ledger records fault-matrix as PASS and names two directories. A PASS row is a claim; rebuilding the 18 by 10 structure from the raw results is what tests it.

structure.howTheGridWasChecked: Grouped each run by point and by occurrence. Both give 18 distinct points and occurrences 1 through 10, with 18 entries at every occurrence, and 180 distinct point-occurrence pairs. So the grid is complete with no duplicates and no gaps.
structure.aNamingNote: The distinguishing column is called occurrence, not repeat. Grouping by repeat gave a single value and looked like a missing dimension until the field name was read.

semantics.faultWritten: faultHitWritten true in all 360 entries, so every point actually injected its fault rather than exiting early
semantics.exitCodes: exception mode 1 in all 180; halt mode 137 in all 180
semantics.whyTheCodesDiffer: halt is SIGKILL, so 137. The exception path leaves the JVM through a normal non-zero exit.

oneFieldThatLooksLikeAFailureAndIsNot.observation: Every exception-mode entry records exitCode 1 against expectedExit -1 while still passing.
oneFieldThatLooksLikeAFailureAndIsNot.resolution: Read the driver at tools/Test-S5Faults.ps1. Expected exit is set per mode as 137 for halt and -1 for exception, and the pass condition is code -eq 137 for halt and code -ne 0 for exception. So -1 in that column documents the expectation 'any non-zero' rather than a literal exit status, and 1 satisfies it.
oneFieldThatLooksLikeAFailureAndIsNot.theRecordedCodeIsTheRealOne: The driver reads the child's status from the exit-code.txt witness the task writes, because the Gradle wrapper itself always exits 0. Grading on the wrapper's code would have made every point fail, which is why the witness exists.

conclusion: Goal item 4 is as described. Two independent 18 by 10 runs, 360 points, every one injecting its fault with no timeout, and exit codes that match each mode's rule.
